## The Model

The **Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) model**, introduced by Black and Scholes and
by Merton in 1973, is a **constant volatility model** for a financial market.
It is a cornerstone of [[quantitative-finance]], in particular of
[[option-pricing]], where it describes the dynamics of the underlying assets
of derivatives such as [[derivatives|options]].

:::{.definition data-title="Black-Scholes-Merton Model"}

The BSM model consists of two assets, a risk-free asset $B$ and a risky asset
(stock) $S$ with price dynamics given by

$$
\begin{align}
dB_t & = rB_t\,dt, \\
dS_t & = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t,
\end{align}
$$

where $r$, $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are deterministic constants and $W$ is a
Brownian motion. Here $r$ is the **risk-free interest rate**, $\mu$ is the
**drift coefficient** and $\sigma$ is the **diffusion coefficient**
(the **volatility**).

:::

The model assumes that

- the interest rate, drift and volatility are constant,
- the stock pays no dividends (see [[black-scholes-model-with-dividends]]),
- trading is continuous and there are no transaction costs,
- assets are infinitely divisible and short selling is allowed.

## Solution and Properties

The risk-free asset solves $B_t = B_0e^{rt}$, and the stock follows
[[geometric-brownian-motion]] with solution

$$
S_t = S_0\exp\left( \left( \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)t + \sigma W_t \right).
$$

Here $\mathcal{N}(m,v)$ denotes the normal distribution with mean $m$ and
variance $v$ (not to be confused with the function $N(x)$, the standard normal
cumulative distribution function used in the pricing formulas in
[[european-options]]). Since $W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,t)$, the stock price is
**log-normally** distributed,

$$
\log S_t \sim \mathcal{N}\left( \log S_0 + \left( \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)t,\;
\sigma^2 t \right),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0e^{\mu t}.
$$

In particular the price stays positive, and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation
of the log-returns per unit of $\sqrt{t}$.

## Risk-Neutral Dynamics

Under the risk-neutral measure $\mathbb{Q}$ the discounted stock price
$e^{-rt}S_t$ is a [[martingale-theory|martingale]], so the drift $\mu$ is
replaced by $r$,

$$
dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t^{\mathbb{Q}},
\qquad
S_T = S_0\exp\left( \left( r - \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)T
+ \sigma W_T^{\mathbb{Q}} \right).
$$

Here $W^{\mathbb{Q}}_t = W_t + \frac{\mu - r}{\sigma}t$ is a Brownian motion
under $\mathbb{Q}$. The change of measure, via [[girsanov-theorem]] and the
[[radon-nikodym-derivative]], is constructed in [[risk-neutral-pricing]].
Note that the volatility $\sigma$ is the same under $\mathbb{P}$ and
$\mathbb{Q}$.

## Black-Scholes PDE

Consider a derivative with payoff $h(S_T)$ whose price at time $t$ is
$V(t,S_t)$. The idea of Black-Scholes is to **delta-hedge**: trade the
underlying stock to eliminate the randomness in the value of the option.

Hold one option together with $\Delta_t$ shares of stock and $\alpha_t$ units
of the bond, with value

$$
\Pi_t = V(t,S_t) + \Delta_tS_t + \alpha_tB_t.
$$

Choose the hedge to be **self-financing**, that is the value changes only
through changes in the asset prices and no money is added or removed, so

$$
d\Pi_t = dV + \Delta_t\,dS_t + \alpha_t\,dB_t.
$$

By [[ito-formula]], the option price satisfies

$$
dV = \left( \partial_t V + \mu S_t\,\partial_S V
+ \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S_t^2\,\partial_{SS}V \right)dt
+ \sigma S_t\,\partial_S V\,dW_t.
$$

Substituting the dynamics of $S$ and $B$,

$$
d\Pi_t = \left( \partial_t V + \mu S_t(\partial_S V + \Delta_t)
+ \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S_t^2\,\partial_{SS}V + \alpha_trB_t \right)dt
+ \sigma S_t(\partial_S V + \Delta_t)\,dW_t.
$$

We choose $\Delta_t = -\partial_S V$ so that the coefficient of $dW_t$ is zero.
The drift of the stock $\mu$ also cancels, leaving

$$
d\Pi_t = \left( \partial_t V + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S_t^2\,\partial_{SS}V
+ \alpha_trB_t \right)dt.
$$

The portfolio $\Pi_t = V - S_t\,\partial_S V + \alpha_tB_t$ is now
deterministic over $dt$, so to avoid arbitrage it must grow at the risk-free
rate, $d\Pi_t = r\Pi_t\,dt$. Equating the two expressions for $d\Pi_t$, the
$\alpha_trB_t$ terms cancel and we obtain the Black-Scholes PDE.

:::{.definition data-title="Black-Scholes Equation"}

Consider a derivative on a stock paying no dividends with maturity $T$ and
payoff $h(S_T)$. Its price $V(t,S)$ satisfies

$$
\begin{cases}
\partial_t V + \dfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\,\partial_{SS}V
+ rS\,\partial_S V - rV = 0, \\[1ex]
V(T,S) = h(S) \quad \text{for all } S,
\end{cases}
$$

where $r$ is the risk-free interest rate and $\sigma$ is the volatility of the
stock.

:::

Note that the drift $\mu$ does not appear: the price of the option does not
depend on the expected return of the stock. This is the same reason the
risk-neutral measure replaces $\mu$ by $r$.

**Interpretation.** Rewrite the PDE as

$$
\partial_t V + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\,\partial_{SS}V
= r\left( V - S\,\partial_S V \right).
$$

The right-hand side is the return, over an infinitesimal period, on the cash
position: the option premium minus the amount spent on the hedging shares,
times the interest rate. The left-hand side is the change in value of the
delta-hedged option. The first term captures the effect of the shortening
maturity (theta) and the second the effect of the curvature (gamma), which is
the risk that remains after the delta is hedged. In terms of the Greeks (see
[[option-greeks]]),

$$
\Theta + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\,\Gamma + rS\,\Delta - rV = 0.
$$

The PDE can be reduced to the [[diffusion-equation]] (heat equation) by a
change of variables, and by the [[feynman-kac-formula]] its solution is the
risk-neutral expectation $e^{-r(T-t)}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[h(S_T)\mid S_t]$.

## Option Pricing

For an option with payoff $h(S_T)$ at maturity $T$ the model gives two
equivalent ways to find the fair price, both developed in
[[option-pricing]]:

- **PDE approach**: build a self-financing portfolio of stock and bond that
  replicates the payoff. No arbitrage then forces the price to solve the
  Black-Scholes PDE above.
- **Risk-neutral approach**: the price at time $0$ is the discounted expected
  payoff under $\mathbb{Q}$,
  $$
  e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[h(S_T)].
  $$

For European calls and puts these give closed-form prices. See
[[european-options]]. Their sensitivities are the [[option-greeks]].

## Multi-Asset Model

The model has a vector equivalent. Take $d$ risky assets driven by an
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion $W = (W^1,\dots,W^m)$,

$$
dS_t^i = \mu_i S_t^i\,dt + S_t^i\sum_{j=1}^m \sigma_{ij}\,dW_t^j,
\qquad i = 1,\dots,d,
$$

with constant drift vector $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and volatility matrix
$\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$. The solution is

$$
S_t^i = S_0^i\exp\left( \left( \mu_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}\sigma_{ij}^2 \right)t
+ \sum_{j}\sigma_{ij}W_t^j \right).
$$

The log-returns are jointly normal with covariance matrix $\Sigma t$, where
$\Sigma = \sigma\sigma^\top$ has entries $\Sigma_{ik}$ equal to the
instantaneous covariance of $\log S^i$ and $\log S^k$, so correlation between
assets enters through $\Sigma$.

Under $\mathbb{Q}$ every asset has drift $r$. A risk-neutral measure exists
if there is a **market price of risk** vector $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with
$\sigma\theta = \mu - r\mathbf{1}$. The market is arbitrage-free if such a
$\theta$ exists, and complete if in addition $\sigma$ is invertible
($d = m$). This model prices multi-asset options such as basket and exchange
options.

## Limitations and Extensions

The assumption of a constant volatility is not consistent with market
prices. Implied volatility varies with strike and maturity, giving the
volatility smile or surface (see [[volatility-surfaces]]). Models that relax
it include

- [[time-dependent-volatility-model]]: $\sigma = \sigma(t)$,
- [[local-volatility-model]]: $\sigma = \sigma(t,S_t)$, including the
  [[cev-model]],
- [[stochastic-volatility-model]]: volatility is random, such as the
  [[heston-model]],
- [[black-scholes-model-with-dividends]]: a stock that pays dividends.
